Bumrah — the postman who seldom fails to deliver
 Plucked out from anonymity despite an action that could so easily have put the traditionalists off, he took little time to establish himself as a premier paceman; his unique skill-sets allowed him to flourish anywhere in the world, on any kind of track because he can take the pitch out of the equation effortlessly
 Published - November 20, 2026 07:45 am IST - Wellington 
 R. Kaushik READ LATER 
 SEE ALL 
 Remove 
 As Jasprit Bumrah starts his walk-run towards the bowling crease, you brace yourself for the magical. For the out of the ordinary. You prepare to be shocked out of your wits, even though you have seen what he can do, time after time. You don’t dare blink, because you feel an event is about to unfold. An event of great impact and effect, an event to elevate you to a different plane even if you are just a distant bystander, watching the master go about his business as if it were just another day in office.
 There is a reason why Bumrah enjoys the pre-eminent status conferred on him by the pundits, those who have been there and done that. His peers find him an unfathomable riddle; they base their opinion on what they have come up against in their careers. His illustrious seniors, who have a much larger sample size for comparison, are also in awe of his genius, drawn magnetically to the braced left knee, the hyperextended right arm, the metronomic accuracy with which he attacks either the top of the stumps or the toes that stand between the ball and the base of the wickets.
 In a world of chaos and uncertainty, Bumrah is a bank, a postman who mostly delivers and seldom disappoints. India must be thankful they have in their ranks one of the all-time greats, even if his international career is less than 11 years old and even though he is now being managed with great care and diligence so that his protesting body doesn’t pack up entirely and therefore prevents him from turning up for the clashes that truly matter – such as Test faceoffs, or marquee white-ball events such as the World Cups and the Champions Trophy.
 Bumrah has bucked convention in so many different ways that it is hard to know where to begin. There is much that John Wright has contributed to Indian cricket, but none of them will top his unearthing of a rare, unpolished (at the time) gem that has now attained a magnificent sparkle which is the envy of the rest of the world.
 Wright, the pugnacious left-handed opening batter who also led New Zealand with distinction, was India’s first overseas coach. Appointed to that role towards the end of 2000, he oversaw a difficult phase in Indian cricket, mired in the aftermath of the match-fixing scandal of earlier that year that weaned fans away from the sport and left them feeling disillusioned, if not downright cheated. There was anger and despair among the teeming masses who had invested so much in the fortunes of the national team, only to learn that not all of their heroes were driven by the pride and privilege of representing the country and targeting victories.
